Let us analyze how a set \(S\) can have cousins.

Since each element \(s\in S\) must pair with either \(s-1\) or \(s+1\), no element of \(S\) can have both neighbors in \(S\). Thus \(S\) has no run of three consecutive integers. Its maximal consecutive blocks have length either \(1\) or \(2\).

- A length-\(2\) block \(\{a,a+1\}\) forces \(a\) to pair with \(a-1\) and \(a+1\) to pair with \(a+2\). So both choices are forced.
- A length-\(1\) block \(\{a\}\) may pair with either \(a-1\) or \(a+1\).

Consider chains of blocks separated by exactly one missing integer. If a chain contains a length-\(2\) block, all choices in that chain become forced, so the chain contributes at most \(1\) cousin. Such chains do not help create the factor \(4040>1\), so for a minimal example we only use chains of length-\(1\) blocks.

A chain of \(m\) singleton blocks has the form
\[
a,\ a+2,\ a+4,\ldots,a+2(m-1).
\]

\[
\text{left, left, }\ldots\text{, left, right, right, }\ldots\text{, right}.
\]
There are exactly \(m+1\) valid choices. Thus a singleton chain of size \(m\) contributes \(m+1\) cousins and uses \(m\) elements of \(S\).

Therefore, if the chains have sizes \(m_1,m_2,\ldots\), then
\[
4040=\prod (m_i+1)

|S|=\sum m_i.
